Subjects
Main
Protein engineering underpins modern biotechnology, enabling the development of high-performance proteins for therapeutic and industrial applications, including genome-editing effectors1,2. Traditional strategies, including rational design, site-directed mutagenesis and directed evolution, have yielded important advances but remain labor intensive and dependent on detailed structural or mechanistic knowledge3. More recently, machine learning has enabled in silico prediction of mutational effects and accelerated protein optimization4,5. Methods such as EVOLVEpro, AiCE and MULTI-Evolve use active learning with protein language models (PLMs) or inverse folding (IF) approaches to guide mutagenesis6,7,8, while related efforts have addressed complementary challenges including protospacer-adjacent motif reprogramming and de novo CRISPR effector design9,10,11. Despite these advances, most existing strategies require large task-specific training datasets or exhibit uncertain transferability across related protein families. A central bottleneck in protein engineering is that most newly discovered protein families lack sufficient experimental data for artificial intelligence (AI)-driven optimization and evolution. This limitation constrains both traditional and computational approaches and highlights the need for data-efficient frameworks capable of leveraging sparse measurements to guide experimentally tractable optimization across related protein scaffolds4,7.
To address this challenge, we focused on Fanzor nucleases, a recently discovered family of compact, eukaryotic programmable nucleases that remains largely unexplored by data-driven engineering approaches compared with other CRISPR systems12,13. Among these, Fanzor2 (Fz2) nucleases, typically under 500 aa, are RNA-guided DNA endonucleases encoded in eukaryotic genomes and are well suited for single-AAV delivery14. Although certain eukaryotic Fz2 variants exhibit broader target-adjacent motif (TAM) flexibility than other compact nucleases15,16,17, achieving consistently high editing activity in bulk mammalian cells has remained challenging. Recent efforts have improved select Fz2 orthologs but have largely relied on scaffold-specific strategies and targeted enrichment18,19. These observations highlight the need for expanded discovery of functional eukaryotic Fz2 orthologs and adaptive model-guided frameworks capable of optimizing diverse scaffolds under sparse experimental constraints.
Here, we address these challenges through an integrated discovery and model-guided engineering framework. We first computationally prioritized and experimentally validated several active eukaryotic Fz2 orthologs from a pool of over 1,600 candidates, expanding the repertoire of functionally characterized Fz2 nucleases. We then developed EvoMax, a protein engineering pipeline that integrates transfer-learning Gaussian process regression (GPR), a PLM (ESM-2) and an IF model (ESM-IF) to prioritize candidate mutations7,20,21. Using this framework, we systematically optimized the effector protein in combination with parallel engineering of the ωRNA scaffold to generate FanzMAX v3-hLa. The final system achieved an approximately tenfold increase in endogenous editing efficiency, reaching up to 97% with a mean editing activity of ~33% across 19 loci in bulk mammalian cells, surpassing previously established benchmarks18,22. The optimized variant also exhibited expanded TAM compatibility, broadening the targeting scope of Fz2s. EvoMax-guided optimization further enabled functional rescue of multiple inactive Fz2 orthologs, supporting transfer of learned fitness constraints within this protein family. Lastly, we demonstrated in vivo genome editing by targeting hPCSK9 in mice using single-AAV delivery. These results demonstrate that coordinated ωRNA scaffold engineering and model-guided protein optimization can substantially improve compact eukaryotic Fz2 nuclease activity, yielding FanzMAX variants with enhanced editing efficiency and therapeutic potential.
Results
Systematic screening and functional characterization of eukaryotic Fz2 orthologs
Although several eukaryotic Fz2 systems have been reported, including NlovFz2, genome-editing activity in unselected bulk mammalian cells has generally remained modest, with high efficiencies often requiring cell-sorting enrichment18,19,23. To identify Fanzor effectors that combine high potency with compact size suitable for single-AAV delivery, we performed a systematic bioinformatic expansion of the Fz2 family (Supplementary Methods), identifying over 1,600 Fz2-like sequences spanning broad evolutionary diversity (Extended Data Fig. 1)16,23. From this dataset, we prioritized 332 eukaryotic orthologs for high-resolution taxonomic and phylogenetic analysis (Fig. 1a). To identify candidates with enhanced cleavage activity, we selected seven representative orthologs from distinct phylogenetic subclusters for functional validation. Using an in vitro transcription–translation (IVTT)-based TAM screening assay, we evaluated their DNA cleavage activity and TAM preferences (Fig. 1b)24. Among these candidates, the ortholog M7 exhibited robust cleavage activity with a 5′-CCG-3′ TAM preference (Fig. 1c). Therefore, we expanded our analysis to nine additional orthologs within the M7-related subcluster, leading us to select a previously cataloged eukaryotic Fz2 ortholog from Naegleria lovaniensis (XP_044555062.1; hereafter referred to as NaloFz2)12 for functional characterization. NaloFz2 displayed clear biochemical activity in vitro while exhibiting a 5′-CCG-3′ TAM preference (Fig. 1c). Comparative sequence analysis of the M7-related subcluster revealed substantial structural heterogeneity at the N-terminus. Whereas the catalytic RuvC domain and predicted DNA-binding regions were highly conserved, the N-terminal domain (NTD) showed variable integrity, ranging from fully preserved to partially truncated or entirely absent (Fig. 1d and Extended Data Fig. 2). This structural divergence correlated with functional capacity; detectable in vitro DNA cleavage and TAM identification were observed only among candidates retaining intact NTDs, whereas candidates with truncated or missing NTDs were uniformly inactive.
To assess their activity in human cells, we used a fluorescence-based reporter assay in HEK293T cells in which mCherry expression is restored following Fz2-mediated double-strand breaks (DSBs) and subsequent single-strand annealing repair (Fig. 1e). Using a CXCR4 target site (site 1) containing a 5′-ACCG TAM, both NaloFz2 and M7 exhibited detectable genome editing, with NaloFz2 producing substantially higher reporter activation (Fig. 1f)25. Notably, deletion of as few as 20–30 N-terminal residues abolished NaloFz2-mediated editing, establishing the NTD as a necessary functional module in eukaryotic Fz2 proteins (Fig. 1f). In viral Fzs, such as ApmFNuc, NTDs have been proposed to function as nuclear localization signals (NLSs)23. However, computational analysis failed to identify strong, positively charged NLS motifs within the N-terminal regions of the eukaryotic candidates tested (Supplementary Fig. 1). These results suggest that the NTD of eukaryotic Fz2 orthologs may instead serve a structural scaffolding role required for productive ribonucleoprotein assembly and genome editing in mammalian cells14,23. Despite possessing an intact NTD, NaloFz2 exhibited only modest editing efficiency, indicating that additional constraints, including ωRNA architecture, limit robust activity.
Structure-guided engineering of ωRNA scaffolds
We first used AlphaFold 3 and RNAfold to model the tertiary structure of the NaloFz2–ωRNA–target DNA complex and identify candidate regions for stabilization (Fig. 2a)26,27. The ωRNA scaffold (120 nt in length) consists of three major stem loop (SL) regions, of which distal elements appeared conformationally flexible and made limited protein contacts, suggesting potential sites for engineering. Guided by these predictions, we systematically modified the distal regions of SL1 (C7–U11), SL2 (U44–U46) and SL3 (U81–U90). Substitution of distal loops with GAAA tetraloops revealed that modification of SL3 produced the most pronounced improvement in editing activity. Building on this modification, further truncation of SL3 enhanced activity, whereas SL2 truncation had minimal effect. We further stabilized the truncated scaffold by replacing weak A–U, G–U or U–U base pairs within the remaining helices with G–C or C–G pairs. These combined modifications generated two minimized ωRNA variants, enωRNA v1 (SL3 Δ11 bp GAAA) and enωRNA v2 (SL3 Δ11 bp U–C GAAA), each 92 nt in length, representing approximately three quarters the length of the wild-type (WT) scaffold while exhibiting substantially increased editing activity (Fig. 2b,c). Sequence alignment across orthologs revealed substantial conservation of core ωRNA elements, with partial truncations observed in the ωRNA of M1 and NaloFz2 (Extended Data Fig. 3a). Therefore, we hypothesized that the optimized enωRNA architecture could function across related Fz2 ortholog subclusters. Application of enωRNA v2 enhanced the editing activity of M7 by 8.7-fold and enabled functional rescue of the previously inactive ortholog M9 when the enωRNA v2 scaffold was paired with replacement of its truncated NTD by that of NaloFz2 (Fig. 2d). Together, these results establish enωRNA as a modular and transferable scaffold for enhancing activity across divergent eukaryotic Fz2 orthologs.
In addition to internal scaffold stability, the compact architecture of Fz2 leaves the 3′ spacer region exposed to degradation by cellular exonucleases. Structural analysis indicated limited shielding of this region by NaloFz2 (Extended Data Fig. 3b). Insertion of auxiliary RNA structures did not improve activity (Extended Data Fig. 3c), prompting us to evaluate protein-based stabilization strategies28. Inspired by prime-editing strategies in which the La RNA-binding domain stabilizes 3′ RNA extensions, we tested whether a similar strategy could enhance ωRNA stability29. We evaluated fusions of La orthologs from multiple species to either the N- or C-terminus of NaloFz2. Fusion of human La (hLa) to the C-terminus of NaloFz2 consistently produced the highest editing activity under stringent assay conditions (using CXCR4 site 2), independent of whether enωRNA v1 or v2 was used (Fig. 2e).
A transfer-learning framework for computational evolution of Fz2
To enable efficient mammalian genome editing with NaloFz2, we undertook a systematic protein engineering effort. However, conventional optimization strategies, including experimental directed evolution and rational mutagenesis, are poorly suited to CRISPR nucleases. Directed evolution requires iterative construction of large combinatorial libraries coupled with extensive high-throughput screening, rendering it impractical in mammalian systems (Extended Data Fig. 4)30. Rational design, while structurally informed, often fails to capture the functional complexity of newly identified effectors such as Fz2. Consistent with these limitations, our preliminary analyses indicated that rationally designed NlovFz2 variants showed a low success rate, with only ~25% of mutations improving activity and most being neutral or deleterious (Extended Data Fig. 5a).
To address these constraints, we developed EvoMax, a sequence-informed and structure-constrained framework for identifying beneficial mutations under limited experimental sampling. EvoMax follows a three-component workflow comprising data curation, empirical model selection and hierarchical multiobjective optimization (Fig. 3a). A central challenge in engineering the functionally characterized NaloFz2 is the limited availability of high-quality labeled mutational data. Therefore, we used a transfer-learning strategy and assembled a training dataset of 209 single-point mutations with measured activity values, combining an internal library of NlovFz2 variants with previously published functional datasets (Extended Data Fig. 5a)18. Given the close evolutionary and functional relationship between NlovFz2 and NaloFz2, this strategy captures conserved biochemical constraints across the Fz2 family. During model selection, we benchmarked multiple supervised learning algorithms, including random forest and XGBoost. A GPR model using BLOSUM62-derived encoding demonstrated the strongest empirical performance, achieving an R2 score of 0.693 and a root-mean-squared error (r.m.s.e.) of 0.232 (Fig. 3b,c)20. This model encodes biochemical similarity between amino acid substitutions and serves as the initial empirical component of EvoMax’s two-stage hierarchical selection framework (Extended Data Fig. 5b–e). To efficiently explore sequence space while enabling prioritization beyond the initial labeled set, EvoMax uses an adaptive scoring workflow (Eqs. 1–4). In stage 1, a high-potential shortlist comprising the top 1.5% of candidates is generated using a weighted combination of GPR-predicted activity and ESM-2 evolutionary scores (Eq. 5), with the latter providing priors derived from masked-language modeling by a 650-million-parameter PLM (Fig. 3d,e)21. In stage 2, shortlisted variants are reranked using a structure-informed component (ESM-IF) that evaluates compatibility with the AlphaFold-predicted NaloFz2 backbone, while retaining the contributions from GPR and ESM-2 to integrate empirical, evolutionary and structural information (Fig. 3f and equation (6)). This hierarchical framework prioritizes substitutions that capture shared fitness constraints within the Fz2 family, allowing efficient identification of high-performance variants. EvoMax was applied in successive optimization cycles to iteratively select and validate candidate mutations.
Iterative engineering of NaloFz2 through EvoMax
To evaluate the performance of EvoMax, we conducted three sequential rounds of protein engineering for NaloFz2, using the top-performing variant from each round as the starting point for the subsequent iteration. Across cycles, the relative weighting of empirical prediction, evolutionary priors and structural constraints was adaptively adjusted to balance local optimization with broader exploration of sequence space (Supplementary Fig. 2). In round 1, stage 1 used a 90:10 (GPR:ESM-2) configuration, whereas stage 2 emphasized empirical activity prediction (90% GPR, 5% ESM-IF, 5% ESM-2). In round 2, stage 1 used a 70:30 (GPR:ESM-2) ratio, whereas stage 2 shifted toward structural constraints (90% ESM-IF, 5% GPR, 5% ESM-2). By round 3, stage 1 adopted a 35:65 (GPR:ESM-2) configuration to promote exploration of more distal beneficial mutations, whereas stage 2 increased the evolutionary contribution of ESM-2 to 70%, supported by 25% ESM-IF and 5% GPR (Fig. 4a). Across rounds, this adaptive strategy drove progressive and substantial improvements in genome-editing efficiency, with 10–20 candidates selected per round for validation using a fluorescence reporter assay in HEK293T cells (Fig. 4b). EvoMax consistently produced improved variants across all three rounds, including in round 3 where the starting variant was already highly optimized (Fig. 4b,c). When benchmarked against EVOLVEpro and AiCE predictions on the same round 1 starting background (WT-NaloFz2), EvoMax achieved a higher hit rate for functional variants (84%) compared to EVOLVEpro (20%) and AiCE (35%) (Fig. 4c). The best-performing variants from each round, designated as FanzMAX v1, v2 and v3, exhibited stepwise improvements, culminating in FanzMAX v3, which showed a more than 13-fold increase in mCherry activation compared with WT-NaloFz2 paired with the WT-ωRNA, when combined with the optimized enωRNA v2 (Fig. 4d).
EvoMax-predicted scores showed a modest but significant positive rank association with experimental outcomes across three optimization rounds (Spearman’s ρ = 0.40, P = 0.005, n = 48; Fig. 4e), indicating that the integrated scoring strategy captured experimentally relevant fitness signals despite limited training data. To quantify the contribution of individual modeling components, we performed retrospective ablation analyses against simplified baselines. In round 1, EvoMax scores showed significant association with experimentally measured activity (Spearman’s ρ = 0.49, P = 0.035, n = 19), whereas ESM-2 alone (ρ = 0.20, P = 0.405) and ESM-IF alone (ρ = 0.16, P = 0.511) showed weaker, nonsignificant associations (Supplementary Fig. 3). Because the internal round 1 dataset was limited and the EvoMax configuration was intentionally GPR dominant, we further benchmarked these models across 196 ProteinGym deep mutational scanning datasets31, where EvoMax round 1 modestly but consistently outperformed GPR alone and substantially outperformed ESM-2 and ESM-IF zero-shot baselines (Supplementary Fig. 4). We additionally benchmarked against the BLOSUM62 substitution matrix, which serves as the basis of the GPR kernel; BLOSUM62 alone showed a weak, nonsignificant association with measured activity across the three Fz2 optimization rounds (Spearman’s ρ = 0.14, P = 0.336, n = 48), supporting the conclusion that EvoMax provides value beyond conservative-substitution preference alone. EvoMax operates at the single-site mutation level, with combinatorial variants emerging progressively through iterative stacking across optimization rounds, rather than explicit modeling of higher-order mutational epistatic interactions.
To evaluate endogenous editing performance and decompose the contributions of each engineering layer, we verified the engineered variants at five loci across two cell types (HEK293T and HuH-7), with detailed stepwise comparisons at CXCR4 site 1 and VEGFA site 1 (Fig. 4f,g) and an expanded endpoint comparison at three additional loci (Extended Data Fig. 6). All activities were assessed in bulk cell populations without FACS enrichment to reflect intrinsic editing potency. At CXCR4 site 1, WT-NaloFz2 exhibited 12% indel formation, whereas FanzMAX v3 increased indel frequency to 66% (Fig. 4f). Addition of the hLa domain further enhanced activity, achieving an editing efficiency of 97% in bulk cells (Fig. 4f). Similar trends were observed at VEGFA site 1, where FanzMAX v3 consistently outperformed earlier variants (Fig. 4g). The endpoint component-attribution analysis compared WT-NaloFz2 with WT-ωRNA, WT-NaloFz2 with enωRNA v2, FanzMAX v3 with enωRNA v2 and FanzMAX v3-hLa with enωRNA v2 under matched conditions. Across these analyses, ωRNA scaffold optimization, cumulative protein evolution to FanzMAX v3 and C-terminal hLa fusion each contributed to progressive increases in editing activity. These results support a layered engineering model underlying the final FanzMAX v3-hLa architecture (Fig. 4f,g and Extended Data Fig. 6). Structural mapping of enriched substitutions, including R205, K332 and Q457, revealed localization to key functional regions, including WED and RuvC domains and putative DNA interaction interfaces, suggesting improved DNA engagement and stabilization of the catalytic core (Fig. 4h).
Restoration and secondary optimization of dormant Fz2 orthologs
To assess whether EvoMax could support engineering beyond the NaloFz2 scaffold, we investigated its ability to restore activity in naturally inactive Fz2 orthologs (M1–M6 and M8) identified in our initial screening (Extended Data Fig. 2). Despite substantial sequence homology to functional nucleases, these orthologs exhibited no detectable genome-editing activity, likely reflecting accumulated deleterious divergence or structural incompatibility. Building on our discovery that NTD integrity is a key determinant of Fz2 activity, we implemented a hybrid engineering strategy that combined structural domain grafting with model-guided sequence optimization. Truncated or divergent NTDs were replaced with the NaloFz2 NTD to establish a permissive baseline and all resulting full-length chimeras were paired with the optimized enωRNA v2 scaffold for functional testing (Fig. 5a).
EvoMax was then applied to restore activity in these inactive orthologs (Fig. 5b). Candidate substitutions were first globally scored using a 35:65 (GPR:ESM-2) configuration, without imposing stringent filtering thresholds, and subsequently prioritized within a multiple-sequence alignment (MSA) of inactive orthologs and high-activity Fz2 scaffolds. Using this approach, we defined a focused search space of 10–30 highly divergent positions per protein, enriched for sites likely to constrain activity32. Top-ranked substitutions, selected using an ESM-2-dominant adaptive scoring configuration (5% GPR, 90% ESM-2 and 5% ESM-IF), were introduced into full-length chimeric scaffolds. Two to five substitutions were introduced per ortholog (Supplementary Data 2). Our strategy restored measurable activity in several orthologs, including M3, and most prominently, M2, M5 and M8 in HEK293T cells (Fig. 5c). The recovered M2 and M3 scaffolds, hereafter termed enM2 and enM3, were further optimized through additional rounds of EvoMax-guided engineering using the weighting configuration established during the final round of NaloFz2 evolution. These secondary optimization cycles produced high-potency variants with substitutions such as G298A and I368L, which increased activity by 1.9-fold and 2.5-fold, respectively (Fig. 5d,e). Across recovery and refinement stages, 55–70% of the engineered variants exceeded the activity of their corresponding parental chimeras (Fig. 5f,g). These results suggest that EvoMax can facilitate the recovery and refinement of divergent Fz2 orthologs, outcomes that would otherwise be difficult to achieve through manual prioritization alone. We further examined whether the EvoMax-guided optimization strategy extended to the related effector NlovFz2 (refs. 12,18). Integration of structure-guided analysis with EvoMax-based prioritization guided the selection of a four-substitution combination (E199R, H229Y, C326K and K390N) that enhanced NlovFz2 activity (Extended Data Fig. 7a). The optimized enωRNA v2 scaffold and La fusion strategy remained effective in this context, with the best configuration (yLa-NlovFz2max) achieving reporter fluorescence activation exceeding 60% and outperforming previously engineered NlovFz2 variants (Extended Data Fig. 7b,c)12,18. Together, these results demonstrate that EvoMax supports both functional recovery and secondary optimization across sequence-diverse Fz2 scaffolds.
EvoMax enables high-efficiency genome editing and in vivo activity
To comprehensively evaluate the editing efficiency of the engineered NaloFz2 variants, we characterized FanzMAX v3-hLa across multiple endogenous genomic loci in mammalian cells using next-generation sequencing (NGS). Editing efficiencies were compared with WT-NaloFz2 and established compact effectors, including previously published enNlovFz2 and enCnCas12f1, under unselected bulk conditions without cell-sorting enrichment (Fig. 6a,b)18,22. For unbiased comparison, each nuclease was paired with its corresponding RNA scaffold (WT-ωRNA for WT-NaloFz2, enωRNA v2 for FanzMAX variants and published scaffolds for benchmark editors). All systems were evaluated on identical target sequences with matched TAM requirements, eliminating positional and sequence-dependent bias (Fig. 6b). Across eight endogenous targets, including therapeutically relevant loci such as CXCR4, VEGFA, EMX1, PCSK9 and DMD, FanzMAX v3-hLa consistently achieved higher indel frequencies than all comparator systems (Fig. 6b,c). Extending this analysis to 19 genomic loci, FanzMAX v3-hLa reached a mean editing efficiency of 33% ± 6.1% (Fig. 6c), compared to enNlovFz2 at 11% ± 4.1%, enCnCas12f1 at 12.5% ± 3.5% and WT-NaloFz2 at 3.4% ± 0.94%. These values correspond to an approximately tenfold increase in activity of FanzMAX v3-hLa relative to WT-NaloFz2 and a 2.7-fold improvement over engineered benchmarks, according to mean efficiencies (Fig. 6c).
To define the targeting scope, we systematically profiled the TAM preferences using a 5′-ANNG motif library (Fig. 6d). While WT-NaloFz2 exhibited restricted activity, FanzMAX v3-hLa demonstrated a substantially broadened TAM compatibility, maintaining robust activity across diverse internal dinucleotide combinations, including 5′-ACAG, 5′-ACTG and 5′-AATG (Fig. 6d). Indel pattern profiling revealed a predominance of deletion events, with C-terminal hLa fusion increasing both the frequency and the breadth of indel formation relative to the nonfused v3 variant (Fig. 6e). To assess genomic specificity, we performed comprehensive in silico off-target analysis using Cas-OFFinder33, allowing up to five mismatches and one nucleotide bulge (Extended Data Fig. 8a–d). Targeted NGS of the highest-priority predicted off-target sites confirmed that FanzMAX v3-hLa maintained robust on-target activity with minimal off-target editing. At the CXCR4 site, FanzMAX v3-hLa reached on-target activity of 97% ± 1.38%, with most off-target sites remaining below 1.0%. Only two off-target sites showed modest elevation at 2.2% ± 0.76% and 5.0% ± 0.98%, respectively. At the PCSK9 locus, on-target activity reached 67% ± 1.31%, while all off-target sites remained at or below 0.30% ± 0.085%. Similar specificity profiles were observed at DMD and VEGFA sites (Extended Data Fig. 8a–d).
To evaluate in vivo application, we first screened multiple ωRNAs targeting the human PCSK9 gene in HuH-7 cells and identified PCSK9 guide 3 as the most effective, achieving ~30% editing efficiency following plasmid transfection (Fig. 6f). We next translated top-performing NaloFz2 variants into a series of all-in-one AAV architectures. AAV 1.0 used FanzMAX v1 with an N-terminal yLa fusion, whereas AAV 2.0 and AAV 3.0 incorporated C-terminal hLa fusions paired with FanzMAX v2 and v3, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 9a–c). This change in La fusion configuration reflected iterative optimization during AAV development; yLa was the best-performing configuration identified at the time of AAV 1.0 design, whereas subsequent screening identified C-terminal hLa as a more active configuration for later architectures. To directly evaluate La fusion configuration in a matched AAV 3.0 cassette context, we compared N-terminal yLa, C-terminal yLa and C-terminal hLa in HuH-7 cells while holding all other vector, transfection and assay parameters constant. C-terminal hLa produced the highest PCSK9 editing activity and was incorporated into the final AAV 3.0 architecture (Extended Data Fig. 9d). To enhance knockout efficiency, AAV 2.0 additionally incorporated a dual-ωRNA configuration targeting proximal sites to promote larger deletions. All vectors were further optimized through tissue-specific promoter and regulatory element selection to maximize editing efficiency within AAV packaging constraints. In HuH-7 cells, AAV 2.0 architecture achieved a mean indel frequency of ~68% at the PCSK9 locus, while AAV 1.0 and 3.0 achieved 5.2% and 50%, respectively (Fig. 6g and Extended Data Fig. 9e,f). In mice, the AAV 1.0 scaffold (3.7 kb) established a tolerable and effective editing window, achieving ~25% liver editing and a corresponding 34% reduction in circulating PCSK9 without detectable toxicity (Fig. 6h–j). In contrast, the more potent AAV 2.0 and 3.0 configurations resulted in rapid morbidity within 7–14 days following systemic administration (Extended Data Fig. 10a–d). Analysis of repair outcomes in HuH-7 cells and mouse liver samples revealed that small deletions (≤10 bp) accounted for 98% and 89% of edited reads following AAV 1.0 editing, respectively, whereas large genomic deletions (>30 bp) accounted for 27% and 36% following AAV 3.0 editing, respectively (Extended Data Figs. 9e,f and 10e). These observations suggest that excessive nuclease activity and accumulation of large indels may promote DNA damage, potentially contributing to hepatocyte toxicity and reduced terminal editing in the highest-potency cohorts34,35.
Discussion
Protein engineering is increasingly shifting from stochastic search strategies toward predictive paradigms in which biological function is represented as a navigable sequence-to-fitness landscape36. Although experimental directed evolution or site-directed mutagenesis remains the gold standard, its reliance on repeated library construction and screening limits scalability in therapeutic settings where experimental throughput is constrained37. Model-driven optimization faces a complementary constraint: newly discovered CRISPR effector families typically lack the large-scale mutational datasets that existing approaches require. Fanzor proteins, the most recently identified class of RNA-guided nucleases in eukaryotic genomes, therefore provide a useful system for evaluating data-efficient protein engineering strategies. Here, we introduce EvoMax, a systematic framework that addresses these limitations by combining iterative experimental profiling with model-guided prioritization, integrating transfer-learning-based Gaussian process regression with protein language model and inverse-folding priors. Our results suggest that incomplete discovery and insufficient scaffold optimization contribute substantially to the limited activity previously observed for eukaryotic RNA-guided nucleases. A defining feature of the engineered FanzMAX system is its compact size (<500 aa), which enables packaging of a complete genome-editing system into a single AAV vector, a longstanding challenge for Cas9-derived systems38,39. Through EvoMax-guided refinement, FanzMAX v3-hLa achieved high on-target editing efficiencies in unselected bulk mammalian cells and consistently outperformed previously reported compact nucleases across matched targets and TAM requirements. Mechanistic analyses revealed that high activity requires coordinated multilayer engineering. Inactive orthologs frequently harbor truncated or divergent NTDs that may compromise proper folding and ribonucleoprotein assembly. Genomic analysis of these loci (Supplementary Fig. 5) indicated that the apparent truncations reflect a mixture of alternative start-codon annotations and genuine truncations in degenerate copies in the available assemblies, while the catalytic core is conserved in all cases. Thus, the annotation analysis supports heterogeneity in NTD architecture among inactive orthologs, whereas the functional requirement for the NTD is established experimentally by controlled N-terminal deletion in full-length NaloFz2 (Fig. 1f), rather than inferred solely from these annotations. While domain grafting restores a permissive structural framework, full activity emerges only after the introduction of EvoMax-prioritized substitutions distributed across both the NTD region and the catalytic core. In parallel, optimization of the ωRNA scaffold and C-terminal fusion to human La proved critical for RNA stability and editing efficiency. Systematic TAM profiling revealed broadened sequence compatibility for FanzMAX v3-hLa, substantially expanding the practical target space of compact eukaryotic nucleases.
Beyond optimization of a single scaffold, EvoMax supported recovery and refinement across sequence-diverse Fz2 orthologs despite operating under sparse labeled data, a regime that typically limits large-scale screening and supervised deep learning approaches. A substantial fraction of nominated variants improved activity relative to parental scaffolds, supporting EvoMax’s ability to enrich transferable fitness constraints across sequence-diverse Fz2 orthologs. These results suggest that model-guided prioritization can transfer useful fitness information within the Fz2 family. Whether a similar strategy can be extended to unrelated protein classes or to protein families with different structural and functional constraints remains to be established. Several limitations should be noted. First, transfer-learning performance might decline with increasing sequence divergence, and the boundary of effective information transfer remains to be systematically characterized. Second, EvoMax operates at the single-site mutation level and does not explicitly model higher-order epistatic interactions; combinatorial effects are instead incorporated empirically through iterative experimental stacking.
Several other methods for AI-guided protein engineering have recently been described, notably EVOLVEpro, AiCE and MULTI-Evolve. EVOLVEpro relies on iterative active learning with a regression model trained on experimentally generated datasets, whereas AiCE primarily emphasizes inverse-folding-based prioritization (such as ESM-IF and ProteinMPNN) without integrating empirical activity measurements. MULTI-Evolve incorporates combinatorial modeling of higher-order mutational interactions using PLM zero-shot embeddings and neural-network-based prediction. In contrast, EvoMax was designed for experimentally constrained settings with limited labeled data, integrating empirical activity prediction (GPR), evolutionary priors (ESM-2) and structural compatibility scoring (ESM-IF) through an adaptive weighting scheme. The use of GPR further provides uncertainty-aware regression regularized through a biophysically informed prior (BLOSUM62 kernel), reducing overfitting risk in low-data regimes. These features enable efficient prioritization in newly discovered protein families where extensive screening datasets are not yet available.
Despite strong performance in vitro and in cultured cells, our in vivo studies revealed an important constraint on therapeutic translation. The AAV 1.0 configuration defined a tolerable functional window, achieving effective liver editing and robust PCSK9 knockdown while maintaining a repair profile dominated by small indels. In contrast, higher potency AAV 2.0 and 3.0 variants resulted in acute toxicity and lethality, correlating with increased frequencies of large genomic deletions, consistent with observations for other compact nucleases12,17,34. These findings highlight the importance of balancing catalytic efficiency with genomic tolerability in vivo40. Because multiple parameters varied across AAV versions, including La protein identity, fusion orientation, editor variant and ωRNA configuration, future studies will be important for attributing individual contributions to in vivo efficacy and toxicity. The compact size of FanzMAX systems may also be well suited for transient delivery modalities, such as lipid nanoparticle-mediated mRNA delivery, that limit cumulative DNA damage41,42.
In summary, by combining iterative experimental profiling with adaptive model-guided prioritization, EvoMax enables efficient optimization of compact eukaryotic nucleases, establishing a data-efficient framework for engineering them with improved activity and delivery compatibility.
Methods
Systematic identification of Fz2 orthologs
Fz2 candidate sequences were identified through iterative homology searches across all domains of life. Seed sequences comprising known or putative Fz2 proteins were compiled from prior literature, including eukaryotic Fz2 proteins from fungi and protists, bacterial and archaeal TnpB homologs classified as Fz2-like and viral-encoded Fz2 homologs from large eukaryotic viruses.
BLASTp searches (NCBI BLAST+ v2.12) were performed against the National Center for Biotechnology Information nonredundant protein database with an E-value cutoff of 1 × 10−2 to maximize recall of distant homologs in this recently discovered family, with a maximum of 200 hits per query43. For seeds with sparse protein hits, TBLASTN searches against the nonredundant nucleotide database were performed to uncover unannotated genes in metagenomes.
Raw BLAST results were filtered to produce a nonredundant candidate set. Exact duplicates and subsequences contained within longer hits were removed. An identity threshold of 95% was applied over the aligned region, retaining one representative per near-clonal cluster. Sequences shorter than 200 aa or containing internal stop codons were excluded. Candidates were screened for the conserved RuvC catalytic triad (DED) by motif scanning; sequences lacking these residues were excluded. The final dataset comprised ~1,600 high-confidence Fz2-like candidates, predominantly 300–500 aa in length.
EvoMax construction
EvoMax predicts beneficial single-site mutations by combining PLM scores with a GPR trained on experimental activity measurements. Unlike zero-shot approaches that rely solely on PLM fitness scores, EvoMax learns protein-specific activity landscapes from a small number of characterized mutations. The pipeline consists of three components: (1) GPR-based activity prediction; (2) PLM-based mutation scoring; and (3) structure-conditioned filtering.
Training data
The curated GPR training set comprised 209 unique single-site mutations of WT-NlovFz2 with matched activity measurements18. The original replicate-level dataset included previously published measurements with two biological replicates and newly generated measurements with three biological replicates (Extended Data Fig. 5a); replicate-level measurements were collapsed to variant-level fold-change values before model training. Training mutations were selected through structure-guided and evolution-guided rational design and inclusion of previously characterized variants from published studies18. The mutations were distributed broadly across the protein sequence, sampling residues from each major functional domain. Activity was measured using a fluorescence reporter assay and normalized as fold change relative to WT-NlovFz2. The training data had a mean fold change of approximately 0.89, s.d. of approximately 0.43 and range of approximately 0.07 to 2.67, indicating inclusion of both deleterious and beneficial mutations (Supplementary Fig. 6).
GPR
We designed a custom GPR kernel function on the basis of the BLOSUM62 substitution matrix to measure biochemical similarity between mutations. The BLOSUM62 matrix was normalized to the unit interval by min-max scaling. The kernel computes the average normalized BLOSUM62 similarity between the WT residues and between the mutant residues of two mutations, gated by a Kronecker delta that restricts comparisons to mutations at identical sequence positions. Details are provided in the Supplementary Methods.
PLM-based mutation scoring
Mutations were scored using ESM-2 (650 million parameters; esm2_t33_650M_UR50D) using the masked-mutant probability at each position21. The PLM score was defined as the softmax probability assigned to the mutant amino acid when the corresponding position was masked. Higher values indicate that ESM-2 considers the mutant residue more evolutionarily plausible in the sequence context. ESM-2 scores served as an evolutionary prior, thereby penalizing evolutionarily implausible mutations.

In stage 2, scoring was restricted to 10–30 highly divergent residues per protein defined by MSA against high-activity scaffolds and substitutions were reranked using a configuration of 5% GPR, 90% ESM-2 and 5% ESM-IF. For subsequent optimization of enM2 and enM3, stage 1 maintained the 35:65 (GPR:ESM-2) weighting, while stage 2 used 5% GPR, 70% ESM-2 and 25% ESM-IF, reflecting the final NaloFz2 optimization configuration.
For NlovFz2, candidate substitutions were reranked using a weighted geometric combination of the GPR-predicted activity and exponentiated ESM-IF score, with weights of 10% and 90%, respectively. Mathematical details, including kernel equations and normalization procedures, are provided in the Supplementary Methods.
Weights were empirically chosen to balance exploitation of experimentally learned activity signals (GPR) with broader exploration guided by evolutionary (ESM-2) and structural (ESM-IF) priors; as iterative optimization progressed and the input background became more optimized, weights shifted from GPR-dominant toward ESM-2-dominant configurations to promote exploration of more distal beneficial substitutions.
Cloning
Fz2 protein sequences were human codon-optimized using the GenScript codon optimization tool. Fz2 genes and ωRNA scaffolds were synthesized by Twist Biosciences and cloned into expression vectors to generate pDuet-Fz2-ωRNA, pCMV-Fz2 and pU6-ωRNA constructs. The plasmid encoding CnCas12f1 and its corresponding ωRNA (Addgene, 204999) served as a positive control.
DNA fragments were amplified using 2× Phanta Max master mix (Vazyme) in 20-µl reactions containing 1–10 ng of template and 10 µM primers. PCR thermocycling used a 60 °C annealing temperature for 25 cycles (fragments > 2 kb) or 35 cycles (fragments < 2 kb). Purified amplicons were assembled into vectors by Golden Gate cloning. Briefly, 10-µl reactions, comprising 8 µl of purified fragments, T4 DNA Ligase (New England Biolabs) and either BsaI-HFv2 or BsmBI-v2 (New England Biolabs), were thermocycled for 16 cycles between 37 °C and 16 °C (5 min per step), followed by heat inactivation at 60 °C for 5 min.
All constructs were transformed into Stbl3 Escherichia coli using the Mix & Go! transformation kit (Zymo) and selected on Luria–Bertani agar containing 100 µg ml−1 ampicillin. Plasmids were isolated using QIAquick (Qiagen) or Epoch Life Science spin columns and validated by Sanger sequencing and Nanopore sequencing (Azenta Life Science). Supplementary Tables 1–10 provide engineered ωRNA sequences, mutations in NaloFz2 and NlovFz2 variants, on-target and off-target genomic sites and primers, Fanzor2 candidate protein and ωRNA sequences, La amino acid sequences, the AAV plasmid sequence and a construct key. A summary of each engineered variant, including protein version, ωRNA scaffold and fusion configuration, is provided in Supplementary Table 10.
TAM library generation and in vitro cleavage assay
To systematically characterize Fz2 TAM requirements, we performed an IVTT-based cleavage assay24. Fz2 (125 ng) and ωRNA (25 ng) templates were added to PURExpress (New England Biolabs) reactions containing 25 ng of a randomized TAM library plasmid in a 12.5-µl reaction volume. Following a 2-h incubation at 37 °C, reactions were quenched at 4 °C with RNase A (10 ng; Qiagen) and proteinase K (8 U; New England Biolabs), followed by a 5-min incubation at 37 °C. Cleaved DNA was purified and ligated with Illumina adaptors using the NEBNext Ultra II kit. To selectively isolate the cleaved fraction, we used a two-step nested PCR strategy. Resulting libraries were gel-purified and sequenced on the Illumina MiSeq platform (Admera Health). Enrichment scores were determined by normalizing unique TAM frequencies in the captured fraction against the input library. These data were used to generate a position weight matrix, and motif preferences were visualized with WebLogo3 and Krona plots using a custom Python pipeline45,46.
Mammalian cell culture and transfection
HEK293T (American Type Culture Collection, CRL-3216) and HuH-7 (JCRB0403, Fujifilm) cells were maintained at 37 °C with 5% CO2. HEK293T cells were cultured in DMEM supplemented with GlutaMAX (Gibco), 10% (v/v) FBS and 1% (v/v) penicillin–streptomycin. HuH-7 cells were maintained in DMEM containing 4 mM L-glutamine and 1 g L−1 glucose, supplemented with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. Cells were passaged at 80–90% confluency using 0.05% trypsin-EDTA. For all experiments, low-passage HEK293T and HuH-7 cells (P1–P5) were used.
Transfections were performed using TransIT-LT1 (Mirus) or Lipofectamine 2000 (Thermo Fisher) according to the manufacturers’ protocols. For endogenous gene editing, HEK293T cells were seeded in 24-well plates (3 × 104 cells per well) and incubated for 16 h to reach approximately 80% confluency before transfection. Cells were then transfected with 1 µg of effector plasmid and 250 ng of ωRNA plasmid using TransIT-LT1. For PCSK9 guide screening, HuH-7 cells were seeded in 96-well plates (1 × 104 cells per well) and allowed to adhere for 16 h, followed by transfection with 250 ng of effector plasmid and 100 ng of ωRNA plasmid using TransIT-LT1. For fluorescence reporter assays, HEK293T cells were seeded in 96-well plates (2 × 104 cells per well) and transfected using Lipofectamine 2000 16 h after seeding with 250 ng of effector, 100 ng of ωRNA and 50 ng of reporter plasmid. For all endogenous editing and screening experiments, genomic DNA was isolated 72 h after transfection for downstream analysis. For fluorescence-based reporter assays, cells were analyzed by flow cytometry 48 h after transfection.
Genomic DNA extraction and flow cytometry
Genomic DNA was isolated by aspirating culture medium and adding 100 µl of lysis buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.05% SDS and 25 µg ml−1 proteinase K). Plates were incubated at 37 °C for 15 min, followed by heat inactivation at 80 °C for 30 min.
For flow cytometry, cells were detached using TrypLE Express (Thermo Fisher) and resuspended in complete medium. Data were acquired on a CytoFLEX four-laser flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter) and analyzed using FlowJo version 10.8.1. The gating strategy included FSC versus SSC for cell population identification, FSC-H versus FSC-A for doublet exclusion and EGFP or mCherry fluorescence channels for signal quantification. All assays were performed with at least three biological replicates, with a minimum of 10,000 gated events collected per condition. The detailed gating strategy is specified in Supplementary Fig. 7.
NGS
Targeted genomic loci were amplified, purified and quantified for high-throughput sequencing on the Illumina MiSeq platform (Amplicon-SEQ; Admera Health). PCR primers (detailed in Supplementary Table 4) were engineered to include partial Illumina adaptors at the 5′ ends. To enable sample demultiplexing, a unique 6-bp barcode was incorporated between the Illumina adaptor and the locus-specific sequence, allowing for the differentiation of biological replicates and experimental conditions pooled within a single run.
